arXiv:2606.06919v1 [quant-ph] 05 Jun 2026

Scalable Quantum Algorithms for Gutzwiller Projection

Preprint: MIT-CTP/6038
Byungmin Kang1,2, Hyunwoong Kwon2, Vito W. Scarola3 and Kwon Park2 Affiliation: 1Center for Theoretical Physics—a Leinweber Institute, Department of Physics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA Affiliation: 2School of Physics, Korea Institute for Advanced Study, Seoul 02455, Korea Affiliation: 3Department of Physics, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA 24061, USA
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Quantum simulation requires highly accurate input states. Gutzwiller-projected Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) states provide physically motivated input states for solving strongly correlated lattice models, but their preparation on a quantum computer is hindered by the non-trivial nature of the Gutzwiller projection. We construct scalable quantum algorithms for this task by combining a circuit construction for arbitrary BCS states with the amplitude amplification for Gutzwiller projection (AAGP) procedure. AAGP yields a quadratic reduction in the number of projection queries compared with measurement-based postselection and leads to substantially improved fault-tolerant resource scaling. For projected BCS states optimized for the square-lattice tt-JJ model, we find that the projected-state weight decreases exponentially with system size, but the quadratic improvement is still large enough at physically relevant finite sizes to make a decisive practical difference. In particular, for a 100-site benchmark, AAGP reduces the required number of projection queries by about seven orders of magnitude. These results establish AAGP as an enabling input-state preparation protocol for projected BCS states in quantum simulation.

Quantum simulation offers a possible route to studying strongly correlated lattice models on system sizes beyond the reach of exact classical methods [11, 12, 10]. Solving these models will, in turn, aid in predicting quantum materials properties and settling debates over the fundamental nature of quantum states of matter. Examples of debated issues include the properties of quantum spin liquid models of magnetism (as captured by spin lattice models) [46] and the nature of the pairing mechanism in high-temperature superconductors as captured by the Hubbard lattice models [5, 4]. Hubbard models consist of spinful fermions hopping on a lattice with local (typically on-site) repulsion (see Fig. 1a) and are believed to harbor key features of high-temperature superconducting compounds, including pairing that arises solely from repulsion [3]. The Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) wavefunction [6] was designed as a paired state for describing weakly interacting models of low-temperature superconductivity. But the BCS ansatz fails to accurately capture the ground state of the strongly repulsive models of high-temperature superconductors.

Quantum simulation algorithms [12] offer a wealth of outputs that can be used to accurately identify ground states and other properties of otherwise intractable strongly correlated models of materials [34, 43]. For example, variational quantum eigensolvers (VQEs) [38, 43, 30, 8] and quantum phase estimation (QPE) [24, 1] can be used to obtain energy eigenvalues. Dynamics can be accessed with product formulas [27], the linear combination of unitaries method [9], and block-encoding methods [29]. However, all of these methods are sensitive to the choice of the input (initial) state. Choosing initial states close to the exact ground state is crucial for building fast and accurate quantum simulation algorithms.

Useful variational initial states are known for some repulsive Hubbard and related spin models in strongly correlated regimes. Anderson [3] constructed an ansatz for ground states by Gutzwiller projecting the BCS state [this state is often called the resonating-valence-bond (RVB) state]. The Gutzwiller projection operator, 𝒫G{\cal P}_{G}, acts on all lattice sites simultaneously to remove basis states with double occupancy across the entire lattice [18, 19, 20]. The BCS state has tunable parameters to accommodate a broad class of models, while 𝒫G{\cal P}_{G} accounts for strong repulsion. 𝒫G{\cal P}_{G} is consistent with the Hilbert space structure expected from the strongly repulsive limit (see Fig. 1a), where, for strong on-site repulsion, we expect a partitioning between low-energy (singly occupied) states and unwanted high-energy (doubly occupied) states. Small-system numerics [37, 36, 25] show that the RVB state can be an accurate ansatz in strongly correlated regimes, motivating the question of whether it can also be prepared efficiently enough to serve as a useful quantum-algorithm input state.

Two critical issues arise when implementing the Gutzwiller/RVB approach as a quantum-algorithm initial state on large system sizes. First, we need an efficient quantum algorithm to construct the BCS state. On finite-size quantum computers, this task can be nontrivial because the resulting BCS state may not preserve translational symmetry. Second, we need an efficient quantum algorithm to perform the Gutzwiller projection on the BCS state. 𝒫G{\cal P}_{G} can, in principle, be implemented by a method that repeatedly measures double occupancy at every site and post-selects outcomes with no double occupancy [31, 42]; however, this measurement-based approach is highly inefficient because the probability weight of the RVB state within the BCS state, 𝒲{\cal W}, is, as we will show, extremely small. This issue is especially pressing because the real-space RVB state can be parameterized to capture large classes of strongly correlated models that include disorder and a variety of lattice configurations, thus offering a versatile initial state for quantum algorithms on many different models of materials.

To solve this initial-state problem, we introduce and characterize a quantum algorithm dubbed amplitude amplification for Gutzwiller projection (AAGP), Fig. 1b. We propose that amplitude amplification [17, 45, 13, 29] can coherently increase the weight of the Gutzwiller-projected component of the BCS state, yielding the same quadratic query improvement as Grover-style search to speed up the preparation of RVB states. We show that our algorithm requires 𝒪⁡(1/𝒲){\cal O}(1/\sqrt{\cal W}) queries of the BCS state, whereas the measurement-based projection algorithm requires 𝒪⁡(1/𝒲){\cal O}(1/{\cal W}) queries. As a result, we find much more favorable scaling for fault-tolerant implementations by showing that the TT-gate count for the RVB input state on NsN_{s} sites is 𝒪⁡(ln⁡(2/δ)𝒲​Ns2​log2⁡(1/ϵ)){\cal O}\left(\frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{\sqrt{\cal W}}N_{s}^{2}\log_{2}(1/\epsilon)\right), where δ\delta and ϵ\epsilon are the tolerance and precision, respectively. As an example, we show numerically that using AAGP to prepare the RVB state on the 100-site tt-JJ model (a model that is a limiting case of the Hubbard model) requires ∼107\sim 10^{7} fewer queries than the measurement-based projection algorithm.

The significance of this reduction is not merely asymptotic. In the parameter regime benchmarked here, the quadratic improvement translates into many orders of magnitude in the number of required queries and can move projected-state preparation from effectively unusable to plausibly deployable within a larger fault-tolerant workflow. In this sense, the gain is sufficient to cross a practical finite-size threshold even though the overall scaling remains governed by the exponentially small RVB weight. This finite-size threshold is important because system sizes on the order of 100 sites are already well beyond the exact-diagonalization regime used to calibrate the ansatz and the overlap scaling, while also being large enough to probe physically relevant many-body behavior. We therefore do not view AAGP merely as an abstract quadratic improvement, but as an enabling input-state preparation primitive for physically motivated projected BCS/RVB states.

AAGP can be used to prepare input states for many different lattice models. The test case discussed here is the square-lattice tt-JJ model. But the quantum algorithm we implement for the BCS ansatz allows a versatile set of input parameters. Translational symmetry is not assumed. Real-space and disordered models may therefore be implemented. The AAGP algorithm also accommodates different lattice geometries, including colored inter-site hopping parameters. The filling (defined as half the number of particles per lattice site) can also be tuned. At half-filling, related projected fermionic states can also serve as useful variational states for some frustrated quantum antiferromagnets [5], including cases where spin-liquid ground states are actively discussed [16, 35]. A notable example is the Dirac spin liquid, which is essentially the Gutzwiller-projected Fermi sea filled to the Dirac nodes [44, 22]. Dirac spin liquids are regarded as one of the most promising candidates for the ground state of frustrated spin-1/2 systems, such as on the kagome lattice [39, 21]. The AAGP algorithm therefore provides a versatile class of input states whose preparation is substantially more resource-efficient than measurement-based postselection.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section I describes the overall structure of the AAGP algorithm. Section II explains how to construct the BCS state via the Bloch-Messiah decomposition. Section III explains how to perform the Gutzwiller projection via amplitude amplification. Section IV calculates the probability weight of the RVB state within the BCS state to estimate the quantum advantage of the amplitude amplification algorithm. We conclude in Sec. V.

I Overall structure

The RVB state can be constructed by applying the Gutzwiller projection operator, 𝒫G{\cal P}_{\rm G}, to the BCS state:

|ψRVB⟩=𝒞𝒫G​|ψBCS⟩,|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle={\cal C}{\cal P}_{\rm G}|\psi_{\rm BCS}\rangle, (1)

where 𝒞{\cal C} is the normalization constant. In a straightforward approach, 𝒫G\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{G}} can be implemented by performing projective measurements at every site to remove all configurations with double occupancy. Specifically, the following quantum circuit can implement 𝒫G\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{G}} by applying the CCNOT gates to every pair of neighboring qubits representing the spin-up and spin-down states at each site:

where NsN_{s} denotes the total number of sites. When the measurement outcome in the ancilla qubits becomes a null vector, i.e., 𝒎=0⊗Ns\bm{m}=0^{\otimes N_{s}}, we obtain the RVB state, i.e., |Ψ𝒎=0Ns⟩∝|ΨRVB⟩|\Psi_{\bm{m}=0^{N_{s}}}\rangle\propto|\Psi_{\textrm{RVB}}\rangle.

The measurement-based projection algorithm is conceptually natural but inefficient in practice. Because of the destructive nature of the measurement, any measurement ”failure” with only a single outcome of 1 leads to the collapse of the entire wave function outside the Gutzwiller-projected Hilbert space. Thus, whenever postselection fails, the protocol must restart from the initial state, typically the vacuum or the null state |𝟎⟩=|0⟩⊗N|{\bf 0}\rangle=|0\rangle^{\otimes N} (N=2​NsN=2N_{s}), and regenerate the BCS state by applying the unitary operator 𝒰BCS\mathcal{U}_{\textrm{BCS}}. As a result, the measurement-based projection algorithm requires executing 𝒰BCS\mathcal{U}_{\textrm{BCS}} a number of times inversely proportional to the probability weight of the RVB state within the BCS state, which is exponentially suppressed as the system size increases. In other words, the success probability of the measurement-based projection algorithm is extremely low in any reasonably large systems, as noted in the previous works [31, 42].

In this context, it is vital to develop an alternative quantum algorithm that can systematically raise the success probability of the Gutzwiller projection close to one at will. In this work, we employ the recently developed amplitude amplification method [45, 13, 29] to construct scalable quantum algorithms for the Gutzwiller projection, which can guarantee an arbitrarily high success probability of the Gutzwiller projection while using significantly fewer 𝒰BCS\mathcal{U}_{\textrm{BCS}} and 𝒰BCS†\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}_{\textrm{BCS}} than the measurement-based projection algorithm.

Figure 2 shows the overall structure of the AAGP algorithm. The essence of the amplitude amplification algorithm (or quantum signal processing in general) can be understood in terms of Grover’s quantum search algorithm, which provides a quadratic speedup over the measurement-based search. Then, the AAGP algorithm can generate the RVB state to within δ\delta using only 𝒪⁡(1/𝒲){\cal O}(1/\sqrt{{\cal W}}) applications of 𝒰BCS\mathcal{U}_{\textrm{BCS}} and 𝒰BCS†\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}_{\textrm{BCS}}, together with the conditional unitaries introduced below. This provides a quadratic improvement over the measurement-based projection algorithm, which requires 𝒪⁡(1/𝒲){\cal O}(1/{\cal W}) applications. Details of the AAGP algorithm are provided in the sections below.

II Construction of the BCS state

In this section, we describe how to prepare an arbitrary BCS state using a unitary quantum circuit. Although related constructions have appeared in the literature [23], we provide a step-by-step derivation because this preparation procedure is a key primitive for the quantum algorithms developed in this work.

The BCS state is the ground state of the BCS Hamiltonian, which can be expressed in real space as the Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) Hamiltonian:

HBdG\displaystyle H_{\rm BdG} =∑i,j=1NMi​j​ci†​cj+12​∑i,j=1N(Δi​j​ci†​cj†+H.c.)\displaystyle=\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}M_{ij}c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{j}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}\big(\Delta_{ij}c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{j}^{\dagger}+\textrm{H.c.}\big)
=12​(𝐜†𝐜)​𝐇​(𝐜𝐜†)+(c-number),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\mathbf{c}^{\dagger}&\mathbf{c}\end{array}\right){\bf H}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\mathbf{c}\\ \mathbf{c}^{\dagger}\end{array}\right)+(\textrm{c-number}),

where 𝐜=(c1,⋯,cN)\mathbf{c}=(c_{1},\cdots,c_{N}) with NN being the number of states distinguished by both site and spin indices, i.e., N=2​NsN=2N_{s}. Meanwhile, the single-particle Hamiltonian matrix 𝐇{\bf H} is given as follows:

𝐇=(𝐌𝚫−𝚫∗−𝐌∗),\displaystyle{\bf H}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\mathbf{M}&\mathbf{\Delta}\\ -\mathbf{\Delta}^{*}&-\mathbf{M}^{*}\end{array}\right),

where 𝐌=[Mi​j]\mathbf{M}=[M_{ij}] and 𝚫=[Δi​j]\mathbf{\Delta}=[\Delta_{ij}] are complex matrices satisfying 𝐌†=𝐌\mathbf{M}^{\dagger}=\mathbf{M} and 𝚫t=−𝚫\mathbf{\Delta}^{t}=-\mathbf{\Delta}, which implies that HBdGH_{\rm BdG} is Hermitian. It is important to note that the BdG Hamiltonian in Eq. (II) can describe the Dirac Fermi sea state in the kagome lattice by choosing 𝐌\mathbf{M} appropriately while setting 𝚫\mathbf{\Delta} to zero.

We can obtain the BCS state by exactly diagonalizing 𝐇{\bf H}:

𝐖†​𝐇𝐖=diag​(ϵ1,⋯,ϵN,−ϵ1,⋯,−ϵN),\mathbf{W}^{\dagger}{\bf H}\mathbf{W}=\textrm{diag}\left(\epsilon_{1},\cdots,\epsilon_{N},-\epsilon_{1},\cdots,-\epsilon_{N}\right), (8)

with

𝐖=(𝐔𝐕∗𝐕𝐔∗)\mathbf{W}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}{\bf U}&{\bf V}^{*}\\ {\bf V}&{\bf U}^{*}\end{array}\right) (9)

where 𝐔{\bf U} and 𝐕{\bf V} are two N×NN\times N matrices such that

𝐔†​𝐔+𝐕†​𝐕=𝟏N×N,𝐔𝐔†+𝐕∗​𝐕t=𝟏N×N,\displaystyle{\bf U}^{\dagger}{\bf U}+{\bf V}^{\dagger}{\bf V}={\bf 1}_{N\times N},\;\;\;\;{\bf U}{\bf U}^{\dagger}+{\bf V}^{*}{\bf V}^{t}={\bf 1}_{N\times N},
𝐔t​𝐕+𝐕t​𝐔=𝟎N×N,𝐔𝐕†+𝐕∗​𝐔t=𝟎N×N,\displaystyle{\bf U}^{t}{\bf V}+{\bf V}^{t}{\bf U}={\bf 0}_{N\times N},\;\;\;\;{\bf U}{\bf V}^{\dagger}+{\bf V}^{*}{\bf U}^{t}={\bf 0}_{N\times N}, (10)

which implies that 𝐖{\bf W} is unitary. Note that the eigenvalues always appear in pairs with opposite signs.

Performing exact diagonalization of the single-particle Hamiltonian matrix 𝐇{\bf H} in Eq. (8) is not too difficult for finite-size systems because the matrix size of 𝐇{\bf H} is only four times the total number of sites. Therefore, we can perform exact diagonalization of 𝐇{\bf H} on a classical computer and then feed the resulting information into the quantum algorithm to construct the BCS state on a quantum computer.

After exact diagonalization of 𝐇{\bf H}, the BdG Hamiltonian can be written as

HBdG=∑iNϵi​γi†​γi+(c-number),H_{\rm BdG}=\sum_{i}^{N}\epsilon_{i}\gamma^{\dagger}_{i}\gamma_{i}+(\textrm{c-number}), (11)

which gives rise to the BCS state as the unique ground state annihilated by all Bogoliubov quasiparticle annihilation operators γi\gamma_{i} with i∈(1,⋯,N)i\in(1,\cdots,N). Bogoliubov quasiparticle operators, 𝜸=(γ1,⋯,γN)\bm{\gamma}=(\gamma_{1},\cdots,\gamma_{N}) and 𝜸†=(γ1†,⋯,γN†)\bm{\gamma}^{\dagger}=(\gamma_{1}^{\dagger},\cdots,\gamma_{N}^{\dagger}), are related to electronic counterparts via

𝜸\displaystyle\bm{\gamma} =𝐔†​𝐜+𝐕†​𝐜†,\displaystyle=\mathbf{U}^{\dagger}\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{V}^{\dagger}\mathbf{c}^{\dagger},
𝜸†\displaystyle\bm{\gamma}^{\dagger} =𝐕t​𝐜+𝐔t​𝐜†.\displaystyle=\mathbf{V}^{t}\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{U}^{t}\mathbf{c}^{\dagger}. (12)

Now, a crucial question is how to construct the BCS state in terms of the 𝐜\mathbf{c} operators.

II.1 Bloch-Messiah Decomposition

The BCS state can be constructed by using the Bloch-Messiah decomposition [7, 40]. Specifically, the BCS state can be expressed as follows:

|ΨBCS⟩=∏i=1nfi†​∏j=1p(uj+vj​fn+2​j−1†​fn+2​j†)​|vac⟩,|\Psi_{\rm BCS}\rangle=\prod_{i=1}^{n}f^{\dagger}_{i}\prod_{j=1}^{p}\left(u_{j}+v_{j}f^{\dagger}_{n+2j-1}f^{\dagger}_{n+2j}\right)|{\rm vac}\rangle, (13)

where |vac⟩|{\rm vac}\rangle indicates the vacuum state void of any electrons. New fermion operators, 𝐟=(f1,⋯,fN)\mathbf{f}=(f_{1},\cdots,f_{N}) and 𝐟†=(f1†,⋯,fN†)\mathbf{f}^{\dagger}=(f_{1}^{\dagger},\cdots,f_{N}^{\dagger}), are related to electronic counterparts via

𝐟=𝐃†​𝐜,𝐟†=𝐃t​𝐜†,\displaystyle\mathbf{f}=\mathbf{D}^{\dagger}\mathbf{c},\;\;\;\;\mathbf{f}^{\dagger}=\mathbf{D}^{t}\mathbf{c}^{\dagger}, (14)

where 𝐃\mathbf{D} is the unitary matrix diagonalizing the Hermitian matrix 𝝆=𝟏N×N−𝐔𝐔†\bm{\rho}=\mathbf{1}_{N\times N}-\mathbf{U}\mathbf{U}^{\dagger} such that

𝐃†​𝝆​𝐃=(𝟏n×n⨁j=1pvj2​𝝈0𝟎m×m),\mathbf{D}^{\dagger}\bm{\rho}\mathbf{D}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}\cline{1-1}\cr\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@intercol&&\\ \cline{1-2}\cr&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil\bigoplus\limits_{j=1}^{p}v_{j}^{2}\bm{\sigma}_{0}\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@intercol&\\ \cline{2-3}\cr&&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil\mathbf{0}_{m\times m}\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@intercol\\ \cline{3-3}\cr\end{array}\right), (15)

where 𝝈0\bm{\sigma}_{0} indicates the zeroth Pauli matrix. Note that the eigenvalues of 𝝆\bm{\rho} consist of nn ones, pp pairs of vj2v^{2}_{j}, and mm zeros, so that N=n+2​p+mN=n+2p+m. Physically, nn represents the number of unpaired occupied states, 2​p2p the number of paired states, and mm the number of unoccupied states. When momentum is well-defined, 𝐃\mathbf{D} simply corresponds to the Fourier transform from 𝐜{\bf c} to 𝐟{\bf f}, in which case Eq. (13) reduces to the standard form of the BCS state written in momentum space. However, keep in mind that we aim to construct the BCS state on finite-size quantum computers that may not necessarily preserve translational symmetry. To this end, we need a general protocol to transform from 𝐜\mathbf{c} to 𝐟\mathbf{f}.

To begin, if 𝐃\mathbf{D} were the identity matrix, the BCS state can be generated using a depth-1 quantum circuit:

|ΨBCSdepth-1⟩=∏i=1nci†​∏j=1p(uj+vj​cn+2​j−1†​cn+2​j†)​|vac⟩,|\Psi_{\rm BCS}^{\textrm{depth-1}}\rangle=\prod_{i=1}^{n}c^{\dagger}_{i}\prod_{j=1}^{p}\left(u_{j}+v_{j}c^{\dagger}_{n+2j-1}c^{\dagger}_{n+2j}\right)|{\rm vac}\rangle, (16)

which requires only single-qubit operations for unpaired occupied states and two-qubit operations for paired states. Of course, 𝐃\mathbf{D} is generally not the identity matrix, and therefore the depth-1 BCS state is not the full BCS state that diagonalizes the BdG Hamiltonian. Fortunately, the full BCS state in Eq. (13) can be obtained from the depth-1 BCS state by applying a series of appropriate unitary operators that transform from 𝐜\mathbf{c} to 𝐟\mathbf{f}.

Transforming from 𝐜\mathbf{c} to 𝐟\mathbf{f} essentially amounts to diagonalizing 𝐃\mathbf{D} via Givens rotations. To be more precise, we need to diagonalize the first n+2​pn+2p columns of the N×NN\times N matrix 𝐃\mathbf{D}. Note that only the fermionic modes with indices from 11 to n+2​pn+2p are used to construct the BCS state. In summary, denoting the first n+2​pn+2p columns of 𝐃\mathbf{D} as 𝐃|n+2​p\mathbf{D}|_{n+2p}, our task is to perform the singular value decomposition of 𝐃|n+2​p\mathbf{D}|_{n+2p} by using an appropriate series of Givens rotations.

Givens rotations can be expressed using the following matrix:

𝐆j,j+1​(θ,ϕ)≡(1⋱𝐆⁡(θ,ϕ)⋱1),\mathbf{G}_{j,j+1}(\theta,\phi)\equiv\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc}1&&&&\\ &\ddots&&&\\ \cline{3-3}\cr&&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil\mathbf{G}(\theta,\phi)\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@intercol&&\\ \cline{3-3}\cr&&&\ddots&\\ &&&&1\end{array}\right), (17)

where

𝐆⁡(θ,ϕ)≡(ei​ϕ​cos⁡θ−ei​ϕ​sin⁡θe−i​ϕ​sin⁡θe−i​ϕ​cos⁡θ).\mathbf{G}(\theta,\phi)\equiv\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}e^{i\phi}\cos\theta&-e^{i\phi}\sin\theta\\ e^{-i\phi}\sin\theta&e^{-i\phi}\cos\theta\end{array}\right). (18)

is located in the 2×22\times 2 diagonal block containing the jj and (j+1)(j+1)-th diagonal elements.

Before applying the Givens rotations, however, it is useful to simplify 𝐃|n+2​p\mathbf{D}|_{n+2p}, which can reduce the number of Givens rotations needed for the singular value decomposition. This simplification is possible because there is a redundancy in the form of 𝐃|n+2​p\mathbf{D}|_{n+2p} that can result in the same BCS state. We can use this redundancy to make [𝐃|n+2​p]i​j=0[\mathbf{D}|_{n+2p}]_{ij}=0 for i−j>N−ni-j>N-n. Please refer to the Appendix A for more information.

It is helpful to understand this redundancy and the subsequent Givens rotations through a simple example. From this forward, let us consider an example with N=6N=6, n=3n=3, and p=1p=1, in which case 𝐃|n+2​p=5\mathbf{D}|_{n+2p=5} can be simplified as

𝐃|5=(∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗0∗∗∗∗00∗∗∗),\displaystyle\mathbf{D}|_{5}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc|cc}*&*&*&*&*\\ &*&*&*&*\\ &*&*&*&*\\ &*&*&*&*\\ 0&*&*&*&*\\ 0&0&*&*&*\end{array}\right),

where ∗* indicates some arbitrary numbers, and the vertical line separates the nn-th and (n+1)(n+1)-th columns. As can be seen, the bottom-left corner of the matrix becomes zero. Note that this simplification is performed at the preparation stage before computing all the necessary Givens rotation angles to construct the BCS state in a quantum circuit.

Next, we need to compute the necessary Givens rotation angles to perform the singular value decomposition of 𝐃|n+2​p\mathbf{D}|_{n+2p}. Let us apply 𝐆3,4​(θ1,ϕ1)\mathbf{G}_{3,4}(\theta_{1},\phi_{1}) to 𝐃|5\mathbf{D}|_{5} as follows:

𝐆3,4​(θ1,ϕ1)​𝐃|5=(∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗𝟎∗∗∗∗0∗∗∗∗00∗∗∗),\displaystyle\mathbf{G}_{3,4}(\theta_{1},\phi_{1})\mathbf{D}|_{5}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc|cc}*&*&*&*&*\\ &*&*&*&*\\ \cline{1-2}\cr\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil*\hfil\lx@intercol&\lx@intercol\hfil*\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@intercol&*&*&*\\ \vrule\lx@intercol\hfil{\bf 0}\hfil\lx@intercol&\lx@intercol\hfil*\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@intercol&*&*&*\\ \cline{1-2}\cr 0&*&*&*&*\\ 0&0&*&*&*\end{array}\right),

where θ1\theta_{1} and ϕ1\phi_{1} are chosen so that the bottom-left element (bold-faced zero) in the 2×22\times 2 box of the right-hand matrix becomes zero. The specific values of θ1\theta_{1} and ϕ1\phi_{1} can be computed in advance on a classical computer and then fed into the quantum algorithm.

The main idea is to repeatedly perform similar Given rotations until the resulting matrix is fully singular-value-decomposed. Again, let us take the previous example and perform the following series of Givens rotations.

↦𝐆2,3​(7)​𝐆4,5​(8)(λ100000λ20¯0¯0¯0𝟎∗∗∗00∗∗∗00𝟎∗∗000∗∗)↦𝐆3,4​(9)​𝐆5,6​(10)(λ100000λ200000λ30¯0¯00𝟎∗∗000∗∗000𝟎∗)\displaystyle\xmapsto{\mathbf{G}_{2,3}(7)\mathbf{G}_{4,5}(8)}\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc|cc}\lambda_{1}&0&0&0&0\\ \cline{2-3}\cr 0&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil\lambda_{2}\hfil\lx@intercol&\lx@intercol\hfil\underline{0}\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@intercol&\underline{0}&\underline{0}\\ 0&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil{\bf 0}\hfil\lx@intercol&\lx@intercol\hfil*\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@intercol&*&*\\ \cline{2-4}\cr 0&0&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil*\hfil\lx@intercol&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil*\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@intercol&*\\ 0&0&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil{\bf 0}\hfil\lx@intercol&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil*\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@intercol&*\\ \cline{3-4}\cr 0&0&0&*&*\end{array}\right)\xmapsto{\mathbf{G}_{3,4}(9)\mathbf{G}_{5,6}(10)}\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc|cc}\lambda_{1}&0&0&0&0\\ 0&\lambda_{2}&0&0&0\\ \cline{3-4}\cr 0&0&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil\lambda_{3}\hfil\lx@intercol&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil\underline{0}\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@intercol&\underline{0}\\ 0&0&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil{\bf 0}\hfil\lx@intercol&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil*\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@intercol&*\\ \cline{3-5}\cr 0&0&0&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil*\hfil\lx@intercol&\lx@intercol\hfil*\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@intercol\\ 0&0&0&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil{\bf 0}\hfil\lx@intercol&\lx@intercol\hfil*\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@intercol\\ \cline{4-5}\cr\end{array}\right)
↦𝐆4,5​(11)(λ100000λ200000λ300000λ40¯000𝟎∗0000∗)↦𝐆5,6​(12)(λ100000λ200000λ300000λ400000λ50000𝟎),\displaystyle\xmapsto{\mathbf{G}_{4,5}(11)}\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc|cc}\lambda_{1}&0&0&0&0\\ 0&\lambda_{2}&0&0&0\\ 0&0&\lambda_{3}&0&0\\ \cline{4-5}\cr 0&0&0&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil\lambda_{4}\hfil\lx@intercol&\lx@intercol\hfil\underline{0}\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@intercol\\ 0&0&0&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil{\bf 0}\hfil\lx@intercol&\lx@intercol\hfil*\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@intercol\\ \cline{4-5}\cr 0&0&0&0&*\end{array}\right)\xmapsto{\mathbf{G}_{5,6}(12)}\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc|cc}\lambda_{1}&0&0&0&0\\ 0&\lambda_{2}&0&0&0\\ 0&0&\lambda_{3}&0&0\\ 0&0&0&\lambda_{4}&0\\ \cline{4-5}\cr 0&0&0&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil 0\hfil\lx@intercol&\lx@intercol\hfil\lambda_{5}\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@intercol\\ 0&0&0&\vrule\lx@intercol\hfil 0\hfil\lx@intercol&\lx@intercol\hfil{\bf 0}\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@intercol\\ \cline{4-5}\cr\end{array}\right),

where 𝐆j,j+1​(i)\mathbf{G}_{j,j+1}(i) is the abbreviation of 𝐆j,j+1​(θi,ϕi)\mathbf{G}_{j,j+1}(\theta_{i},\phi_{i}) with θi\theta_{i} and ϕi\phi_{i} being the Givens rotation angles, 𝟎{\bf 0} is the zero element vanishing due to the suitable choice of Givens rotation angles, 0¯\underline{0} is the zero element vanishing due to the orthogonality between columns, and λi\lambda_{i} is a U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) complex phase. Again, the specific values of θi\theta_{i} and ϕi\phi_{i} can be computed in advance on a classical computer and then fed into the quantum algorithm.

The above series of Givens rotations provides the necessary sequence of unitary transformations mapping from the full BCS state in Eq. (13) to the depth-1 BCS state written as

|ΨBCSdepth-1⟩\displaystyle|\Psi_{\rm BCS}^{\textrm{depth-1}}\rangle
=∏i=1nλi​ci†​∏j=1p(uj+vj​λn+2​j−1​λn+2​j​cn+2​j−1†​cn+2​j†)​|vac⟩,\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}c^{\dagger}_{i}\prod_{j=1}^{p}\left(u_{j}+v_{j}\lambda_{n+2j-1}\lambda_{n+2j}c^{\dagger}_{n+2j-1}c^{\dagger}_{n+2j}\right)|{\rm vac}\rangle, (73)

which is slightly different from the simpler depth-1 BCS state in Eq. (16) to account for the effects of the phase factors λi\lambda_{i}’s.

Finally, our objective is to obtain the full BCS state, starting from the depth-1 BCS state. This can be accomplished by reversing the series of Givens rotations described so far.

II.2 Quantum circuits for the Bloch-Messiah decomposition

Using the Jordan-Wigner (JW) transformation, we can construct quantum circuits for the depth-1 BCS state and the necessary series of Givens rotations to obtain the full BCS state.

First, apart from the unimportant overall phase factor, the depth-1 BCS state in Eq. (73) can be expressed using the JW transformation as follows:

|ΨBCSdepth-1⟩↦JW∏i=1nX^i​∏j=1pF^n+2​j−1,n+2​j​(θj,ϕj)​|0N⟩,|\Psi_{\rm BCS}^{\textrm{depth-1}}\rangle\xmapsto{\rm JW}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\hat{X}_{i}\prod_{j=1}^{p}\hat{F}_{n+2j-1,n+2j}(\theta_{j},\phi_{j})|0^{N}\rangle, (74)

where X^i\hat{X}_{i} is the Pauli X operator acting on the ii-th qubit to create an occupied state, and F^n+2​j−1,n+2​j​(θj,ϕj)\hat{F}_{n+2j-1,n+2j}(\theta_{j},\phi_{j}) is the local two-qubit operator acting on the neighboring n+2​j−1n+2j-1 and n+2​jn+2j qubits to create a paired state, which can be implemented using the following quantum circuit:

where θl\theta_{l} and ϕl\phi_{l} are the Givens rotation angles obtained using the procedure explained in Eqs. (II.1) and (II.1).

Finally, combining the quantum circuits for the depth-1 BCS state with the subsequent Givens rotations yields the full BCS state. To be specific, the quantum circuit for the full BCS state in the preceding example with N=6N=6, n=3n=3, and p=1p=1 can be expressed as follows:

(77)

where F^​(j)\hat{F}(j) and G^​(l)\hat{G}(l) are abbreviations for F^​(θj,ϕj)\hat{F}(\theta_{j},\phi_{j}) and G^​(θl,ϕl)\hat{G}(\theta_{l},\phi_{l}), respectively. For convenience, we will now refer to the entire quantum circuit described above as 𝒰BCS\mathcal{U}_{\rm BCS}.

It is straightforward to generalize the above procedure to compute the total number of two-qubit gates and the circuit depth for 𝒰BCS\mathcal{U}_{\rm BCS} in general situations, both of which are important for estimating the quantum resources required for our AAGP algorithm. Relegating the detailed derivation to the Appendix, the total number of two-qubit gates is (N−n)​(n+2​p)−2​p2(N-n)(n+2p)-2p^{2}, and the circuit depth is N+2​pN+2p. See Appendix B for details.

III Amplitude amplification for the Gutzwiller projection

The amplitude amplification algorithm [45, 13, 29] is basically an extension of Grover’s quantum search algorithm [17]. Here, we review key aspects of the amplitude amplification algorithm. Suppose that we have a unitary operator 𝒰\mathcal{U} that creates a state with a finite overlap with the target state |Φ⟩|\Phi\rangle from the vacuum state |𝟎⟩=|0⟩⊗N|{\bf 0}\rangle=|0\rangle^{\otimes N}:

𝒰⁡|𝟎⟩=𝒲​|Φ⟩+1−𝒲​|Φ⟂⟩,\mathcal{U}|{\bf 0}\rangle=\sqrt{{\cal W}}|\Phi\rangle+\sqrt{1-{\cal W}}|\Phi^{\perp}\rangle, (78)

where 𝒲{\cal W} represents the probability weight of |Φ⟩|\Phi\rangle within the 𝒰\mathcal{U}-operated vacuum state and |Φ⟂⟩|\Phi^{\perp}\rangle is the remaining component perpendicular to |Φ⟩|\Phi\rangle. In our AAGP algorithm, 𝒰=𝒰BCS\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{U}_{\rm BCS} and |Φ⟩=|ψRVB⟩|\Phi\rangle=|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle:

𝒰BCS​|𝟎⟩=𝒲​|ψRVB⟩+1−𝒲​|ψRVB⟂⟩.\mathcal{U}_{\rm BCS}|{\bf 0}\rangle=\sqrt{{\cal W}}|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle+\sqrt{1-{\cal W}}|\psi^{\perp}_{\rm RVB}\rangle. (79)

where 𝒲{\cal W} now specifies the probability weight of the RVB state within the BCS state and |ψRVB⟂⟩|\psi^{\perp}_{\rm RVB}\rangle is the remaining component perpendicular to ψRVB\psi_{\rm RVB} outside the Gutzwiller-projected Hilbert space, i.e., |ψRVB⟂⟩∝(1−𝒫G)​|ψBCS⟩|\psi^{\perp}_{\rm RVB}\rangle\propto(1-{\cal P}_{\rm G})|\psi_{\rm BCS}\rangle.

Our AAGP algorithm systematically amplifies the amplitude of the RVB state using a series of conditional unitary operators for phase rotation that act on the vacuum state and the RVB state, along with 𝒰BCS\mathcal{U}_{\rm BCS} and 𝒰BCS†\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}_{\rm BCS}. Specifically, the conditional unitary operators acting on the vacuum state and the RVB state are defined as follows:

ℛvac​(φ)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\rm vac}(\varphi) =𝟙+(𝕖𝕚​φ−𝟙)​|𝟎⟩​⟨𝟎|,\displaystyle=\openone+\big(e^{i\varphi}-1\big)|{\bf 0}\rangle\langle{\bf 0}|,
ℛRVB​(φ)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\rm RVB}(\varphi) =𝟙+(𝕖𝕚​φ−𝟙)​|ψRVB⟩​⟨ψRVB|,\displaystyle=\openone+\big(e^{i\varphi}-1\big)|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle\langle\psi_{\rm RVB}|, (80)

where the rotation angle φ\varphi is to be determined by the formula derived later in this paper. When φ\varphi equals π\pi, the conditional unitary operators reduce to Grover’s reflection operators. The amplitude amplification algorithm adjusts the value of φ\varphi to reach the target state as efficiently as possible.

Now, the four NN-qubit unitary operators 𝒰BCS\mathcal{U}_{\rm BCS}, 𝒰BCS†\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}_{\rm BCS}, ℛvac​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm vac}(\varphi), and ℛRVB​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm RVB}(\varphi) can be mapped to their corresponding effective single-qubit operators. This mapping is known as qubitization. To understand how qubitization works, let us introduce an orthonormal state to the vacuum state, |𝟎⟂⟩|{\bf 0}^{\perp}\rangle, defined by the following condition:

𝒰BCS​|𝟎⟂⟩=1−𝒲​|ψRVB⟩−𝒲​|ψRVB⟂⟩.\mathcal{U}_{\rm BCS}|{\bf 0}^{\perp}\rangle=\sqrt{1-{\cal W}}|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle-\sqrt{{\cal W}}|\psi^{\perp}_{\rm RVB}\rangle. (81)

Combining equations (79) and (81) gives rise to:

𝒰BCS​(|𝟎⟩|𝟎⟂⟩)=(𝒲1−𝒲1−𝒲−𝒲)​(|ψRVB⟩|ψRVB⟂⟩),\mathcal{U}_{\rm BCS}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}|{\bf 0}\rangle\\ |{\bf 0}^{\perp}\rangle\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\sqrt{{\cal W}}&\sqrt{1-{\cal W}}\\ \sqrt{1-{\cal W}}&-\sqrt{{\cal W}}\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle\\ |\psi^{\perp}_{\rm RVB}\rangle\end{array}\right), (82)

and its inverse relation,

𝒰BCS†​(|ψRVB⟩|ψRVB⟂⟩)=(𝒲1−𝒲1−𝒲−𝒲)​(|𝟎⟩|𝟎⟂⟩).\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}_{\rm BCS}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle\\ |\psi^{\perp}_{\rm RVB}\rangle\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\sqrt{{\cal W}}&\sqrt{1-{\cal W}}\\ \sqrt{1-{\cal W}}&-\sqrt{{\cal W}}\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}|{\bf 0}\rangle\\ |{\bf 0}^{\perp}\rangle\end{array}\right). (83)

Note that both 𝒰BCS\mathcal{U}_{\rm BCS} and 𝒰BCS†\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}_{\rm BCS} can be represented by the same 2×22\times 2 matrix 𝐔⁡(𝒲)\mathbf{U}({\cal W}):

𝐔⁡(𝒲)≡(𝒲1−𝒲1−𝒲−𝒲).\mathbf{U}({\cal W})\equiv\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\sqrt{{\cal W}}&\sqrt{1-{\cal W}}\\ \sqrt{1-{\cal W}}&-\sqrt{{\cal W}}\end{array}\right). (84)

Meanwhile, ℛvac​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm vac}(\varphi) operate on |𝟎⟩|{\bf 0}\rangle and |𝟎⟂⟩|{\bf 0}^{\perp}\rangle as follows:

ℛvac​(φ)​(|𝟎⟩|𝟎⟂⟩)=(ei​φ001)​(|𝟎⟩|𝟎⟂⟩).\mathcal{R}_{\rm vac}(\varphi)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}|{\bf 0}\rangle\\ |{\bf 0}^{\perp}\rangle\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}e^{i\varphi}&0\\ 0&1\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}|{\bf 0}\rangle\\ |{\bf 0}^{\perp}\rangle\end{array}\right). (85)

Similarly, ℛRVB​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm RVB}(\varphi) operate on |ψRVB⟩|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle and |ψRVB⟂⟩|\psi_{\rm RVB}^{\perp}\rangle as follows:

ℛRVB​(φ)​(|ψRVB⟩|ψRVB⟂⟩)=(ei​φ001)​(|ψRVB⟩|ψRVB⟂⟩).\mathcal{R}_{\rm RVB}(\varphi)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle\\ |\psi^{\perp}_{\rm RVB}\rangle\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}e^{i\varphi}&0\\ 0&1\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle\\ |\psi^{\perp}_{\rm RVB}\rangle\end{array}\right). (86)

Again, note that both ℛvac​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm vac}(\varphi) and ℛRVB​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm RVB}(\varphi) can be represented by the same 2×22\times 2 matrix 𝐑⁡(φ)\mathbf{R}(\varphi):

𝐑⁡(φ)≡(ei​φ001).\mathbf{R}(\varphi)\equiv\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}e^{i\varphi}&0\\ 0&1\end{array}\right). (87)

Next, let us consider applying 𝒰BCS\mathcal{U}_{\rm BCS} to |𝟎⟩|{\bf 0}\rangle and |𝟎⟂⟩|{\bf 0}^{\perp}\rangle, and then ℛRVB​(φ1)\mathcal{R}_{\rm RVB}(\varphi_{1}) to the resulting states, which corresponds to the following multiplication:

(|ψ1⟩|ψ1⟂⟩)\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{c}|\psi_{1}\rangle\\ |\psi_{1}^{\perp}\rangle\end{array}\right) =ℛRVB​(φ1)​𝒰BCS​(|𝟎⟩|𝟎⟂⟩)\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}_{\rm RVB}(\varphi_{1})\mathcal{U}_{\rm BCS}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}|{\bf 0}\rangle\\ |{\bf 0}^{\perp}\rangle\end{array}\right)
=𝐑⁡(φ1)​𝐔​(𝒲)​(|ψRVB⟩|ψRVB⟂⟩),\displaystyle=\mathbf{R}(\varphi_{1})\mathbf{U}({\cal W})\left(\begin{array}[]{c}|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle\\ |\psi^{\perp}_{\rm RVB}\rangle\end{array}\right),

where φ1\varphi_{1} is to be determined by the formula derived later in the paper. This is the first step in our series of unitary operations for the amplitude amplification algorithm.

The second step involves applying 𝒰BCS†\mathcal{U}_{\rm BCS}^{\dagger} and then ℛvac​(φ2)\mathcal{R}_{\rm vac}(\varphi_{2}) to the states obtained from the first step:

(|ψ2⟩|ψ2⟂⟩)\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{c}|\psi_{2}\rangle\\ |\psi_{2}^{\perp}\rangle\end{array}\right) =ℛvac​(φ2)​𝒰BCS†​(|ψ1⟩|ψ1⟂⟩)\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}_{\rm vac}(\varphi_{2})\mathcal{U}_{\rm BCS}^{\dagger}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}|\psi_{1}\rangle\\ |\psi_{1}^{\perp}\rangle\end{array}\right)
=𝐑⁡(φ2)​𝐔​(𝒲)​𝐑​(φ1)​𝐔​(𝒲)​(|𝟎⟩|𝟎⟂⟩),\displaystyle=\mathbf{R}(\varphi_{2})\mathbf{U}({\cal W})\mathbf{R}(\varphi_{1})\mathbf{U}({\cal W})\left(\begin{array}[]{c}|{\bf 0}\rangle\\ |{\bf 0}^{\perp}\rangle\end{array}\right),

where φ2\varphi_{2} is again to be determined by the formula derived later in the paper. Afterward, one can repeat these steps multiple times.

Specifically, after the nn-th step, the resulting states are given by

|ψn⟩={αn​|𝟎⟩+βn​|𝟎⟂⟩if n= even,αn​|ψRVB⟩+βn​|ψRVB⟂⟩if n= odd,\displaystyle|\psi_{n}\rangle=\begin{cases}\alpha_{n}|{\bf 0}\rangle+\beta_{n}|{\bf 0}^{\perp}\rangle\qquad\qquad\;\;\textrm{if $n=$ even},\\ \alpha_{n}|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle+\beta_{n}|\psi_{\rm RVB}^{\perp}\rangle\qquad\textrm{if $n=$ odd},\end{cases} (100)

where αn\alpha_{n} and βn\beta_{n} satisfy the following recursion relation:

(αnβn)=𝐑⁡(φn)​𝐔​(𝒲)​(αn−1βn−1),\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\alpha_{n}\\ \beta_{n}\end{array}\right)=\mathbf{R}(\varphi_{n})\mathbf{U}({\cal W})\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\alpha_{n-1}\\ \beta_{n-1}\end{array}\right),

with the initial condition (α0,β0)=(1,0)(\alpha_{0},\beta_{0})=(1,0). Note that, for odd nn, |αn|2|\alpha_{n}|^{2} indicates the success probability of obtaining the RVB state after the nn-th step of the iteration. Similarly, for odd nn, |βn|2=1−|αn|2|\beta_{n}|^{2}=1-|\alpha_{n}|^{2} indicates the failure probability of not obtaining the RVB state after the nn-th step of the iteration.

After doing some simple calculations, the β\beta recursion relation can be derived as follows:

βn=𝒲​(ei​φn−1−1)​βn−1+ei​φn−1​βn−2,\displaystyle\beta_{n}=\sqrt{{\cal W}}\big(e^{i\varphi_{n-1}}-1\big)\beta_{n-1}+e^{i\varphi_{n-1}}\beta_{n-2}, (105)

where (β0,β1)=(0,1−𝒲)(\beta_{0},\beta_{1})=(0,\sqrt{1-{\cal W}}). The final state obtained from the iteration process is αL​|ψRVB⟩+βL​|ψRVB⟂⟩\alpha_{L}|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle+\beta_{L}|\psi^{\perp}_{\rm RVB}\rangle for some odd LL, in which case the failure probability for the RVB state is given as |βL|2|\beta_{L}|^{2}. The amplitude amplification algorithm solves the optimization problem to determine the minimum number of iterations LL and the corresponding optimal angles {φn}\{\varphi_{n}\} that yield a final failure probability below the desired tolerance.

It is possible to obtain a complete analytic solution to this optimization problem based on a groundbreaking work [45]. First, let us choose δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), which sets the desired tolerance. Then, the optimal angles {φn}n=1,…,L\{\varphi_{n}\}_{n=1,\ldots,L} are given by the following expression [45, 13, 29]:

φn=(−1)n−1​ 2​cot−1⁡(1−γ2​tan⁡n​πL),\varphi_{n}=(-1)^{n-1}\,2\cot^{-1}\left(\sqrt{1-\gamma^{2}}\tan{\frac{n\pi}{L}}\right), (106)

where the value of γ\gamma will be determined through the optimization condition described below. With this choice of {φn}\{\varphi_{n}\}, βL\beta_{L} is in turn given as follows:

βL=exp⁡(i​∑n=1(L−1)/2φ2​n)​TL​(1−𝒲/γ)TL​(1/γ),\displaystyle\beta_{L}=\exp{\left(i\sum_{n=1}^{(L-1)/2}\varphi_{2n}\right)}\frac{T_{L}\left(\sqrt{1-{\cal W}}/\gamma\right)}{T_{L}\left(1/\gamma\right)}, (107)

where TLT_{L} is the LL-th Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind, and LL is a specific odd integer that must be determined along with γ\gamma to ensure that the final failure probability falls below the desired tolerance. See Appendix C for the derivation of Eq. (107). Also, see a recent paper that provides a revised proof of the recursion relation [26].

To determine LL and γ\gamma, let us compute the final failure probability:

|βL|2=δ2​|TL​(1−𝒲/γ)|2,|\beta_{L}|^{2}=\delta^{2}\left|T_{L}\left(\sqrt{1-{\cal W}}/\gamma\right)\right|^{2}, (108)

where we have used the condition TL​(1/γ)=1/δT_{L}(1/\gamma)=1/\delta. Since the Chebyshev polynomial satisfies |TL​(x)|≥1|T_{L}(x)|\geq 1 if |x|≥1|x|\geq 1 and |TL​(x)|≤1|T_{L}(x)|\leq 1 if |x|≤1|x|\leq 1 for a real number xx, we can bound the final failure probability to be |βL|2≤δ2|\beta_{L}|^{2}\leq\delta^{2} if 1−𝒲/γ≤1\sqrt{1-{\cal W}}/\gamma\leq 1 holds. This condition can be satisfied if we choose an odd integer LL satisfying

L≥ln⁡(2/δ)𝒲L\geq\frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{\sqrt{{\cal W}}} (109)

for small δ\delta and large LL [45]. See Appendix D for the derivation of Eq. (109).

To demonstrate how the AAGP algorithm works, we present in Fig. 3 the evolution of the success probability |αn|2|\alpha_{n}|^{2} for the case of (δ,𝒲)=(0.4,6.5×10−11)(\delta,{\cal W})=(0.4,6.5\times 10^{-11}), which corresponds to the condition L≥200001L\geq 200001 according to Eq. (109). As one can see, |αn|2|\alpha_{n}|^{2} evolves smoothly to the final success probability |αL|2|\alpha_{L}|^{2}, which falls within the window of (1−δ2,1)(1-\delta^{2},1), while exhibiting some oscillations in the middle of the iteration.

In summary, our AAGP algorithm requires 𝒪⁡(1/𝒲){\cal O}(1/\sqrt{\cal W}) queries of 𝒰BCS{\cal U}_{\rm BCS} and 𝒰BCS†{\cal U}^{\dagger}_{\rm BCS} accompanied by some specific conditional unitary operators, achieving the same quadratic speed-up as Grover’s quantum search algorithm, compared to the measurement-based projection algorithm outlined in Eq. (2). Note that the measurement-based projection algorithm requires 𝒪⁡(1/𝒲){\cal O}(1/{\cal W}) queries of 𝒰BCS{\cal U}_{\rm BCS} and the subsequent measurement of double occupancy.

III.1 Quantum circuits for the conditional unitary operators

In this subsection, we explain how to construct quantum circuits for the conditional unitary operators, ℛvac​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm vac}(\varphi) and ℛRVB​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm RVB}(\varphi).

First, implementing ℛvac​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm vac}(\varphi) is rather straightforward using the CNNOT gate. Specifically, a quantum circuit for ℛvac​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm vac}(\varphi) can be constructed using one ancilla qubit as follows:

where R^|0⟩(φ)\hat{R}_{\left|0\right\rangle}(\varphi) is the phase shift gate that applies a phase shift of ei​φe^{i\varphi} to the ancilla state |0⟩\left|0\right\rangle.

Second, implementing ℛRVB​(φ){\cal R}_{\rm RVB}(\varphi) directly is quite difficult as it requires identifying the RVB state. The entire purpose of the Gutzwiller projection is to identify the RVB state within the BCS state. Fortunately, we can overcome this difficulty by applying the conditional unitary operator for phase rotation on the Gutzwiller-projected state, ℛG​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm G}(\varphi), instead of ℛRVB​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm RVB}(\varphi):

ℛG​(φ)=𝟙+(𝕖𝕚​φ−𝟙)​𝒫G,\mathcal{R}_{\rm G}(\varphi)=\openone+(e^{i\varphi}-1)\mathcal{P}_{\rm G}, (111)

where 𝒫G\mathcal{P}_{\rm G} is the Gutzwiller projection operator that removes all states with double occupancy. It is important to note that ℛG​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm G}(\varphi) is identical to ℛRVB​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm RVB}(\varphi) on the effective two-dimensional Hilbert space spanned by |ψRVB⟩|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle and |ψRVB⟂⟩|\psi_{\rm RVB}^{\perp}\rangle.

Specifically, a quantum circuit for ℛG​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm G}(\varphi) can be constructed using Ns+1N_{s}+1 ancilla qubits as follows:

where it is interesting to note that the upper central part of the circuit, which contains Ns+1N_{s}+1 ancilla qubits, has a structure similar to ℛvac​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm vac}(\varphi), except that the number of qubits here is Ns+1N_{s}+1 instead of N+1N+1. Once again, N=2​NsN=2N_{s} due to the spin degree of freedom.

III.2 Quantum resource requirements

Since many different quantum gates are used in our quantum circuits, it is important to estimate the total quantum resource requirements. To this end, we estimate the number of TT-gates as a measure of the non-Clifford gates required to implement our quantum circuits. Two main non-Clifford gates used in our circuit are single-qubit Pauli rotations and CNNOT gates.

In the current state-of-the-art algorithm [41], a typical single-qubit Pauli zz-rotation requires 3​log2​(1/ϵ)3\log_{2}(1/\epsilon) TT-gates, where ϵ\epsilon determines the precision. As our circuits use many single-qubit Pauli rotations, we assume that each is typical in terms of TT-gate count. The CNNOT gate can be implemented using 2​N2N Toffoli gates and one CNOT gate with NN ancilla qubits [33]. Given that the optimal count of TT-gates for the Toffoli gate is 77 [2, 14], the TT-gate count for the CNNOT gate scales as 𝒪⁡(N){\cal O}(N).

Now, each Givens rotation involves two single Pauli rotations. This means that the quantum circuit for 𝒰BCS\mathcal{U}_{\rm BCS} has a TT-gate count of 𝒪⁡(N2​log2⁡(1/ϵ)){\cal O}(N^{2}\log_{2}(1/\epsilon)) when approximating each Pauli rotation to a precision of ϵ\epsilon. Note that, as shown previously, the number of two-qubit gates in 𝒰BCS\mathcal{U}_{\rm BCS} is (N−n)​(n+2​p)−2​p2(N-n)(n+2p)-2p^{2}, which scales as 𝒪⁡(N2){\cal O}(N^{2}) since both nn and pp scale as 𝒪⁡(N){\cal O}(N).

Meanwhile, the quantum circuit for ℛvac​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm vac}(\varphi) uses two CNNOT gates and one Paili rotation gate, resulting in a TT-gate count of 𝒪⁡(N)+𝒪⁡(log2⁡(1/ϵ)){\cal O}(N)+{\cal O}(\log_{2}(1/\epsilon)). Similarly, the quantum circuit for ℛG​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm G}(\varphi) uses NsN_{s} Toffoli gates, two CNs{}^{N_{s}}NOT gates, and one Pauli rotation gate, resulting in a similar TT-gate count of 𝒪⁡(N)+𝒪⁡(log2⁡(1/ϵ)){\cal O}(N)+{\cal O}(\log_{2}(1/\epsilon)). For large NN, the TT-gate counts for ℛvac​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm vac}(\varphi) and ℛG​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm G}(\varphi) are negligible compared to those for 𝒰BCS\mathcal{U}_{\rm BCS} and 𝒰BCS†\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}_{\rm BCS}.

Finally, the quantum circuit for the AAGP algorithm requires 𝒪⁡(ln⁡(2/δ)𝒲){\cal O}\left(\frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{\sqrt{\mathcal{W}}}\right) queries of 𝒰BCS\mathcal{U}_{\rm BCS} and ℛG​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm G}(\varphi), or 𝒰BCS†\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}_{\rm BCS} and ℛvac​(φ)\mathcal{R}_{\rm vac}(\varphi). This means that the total TT-gate count of the quantum circuit for the RVB state is 𝒪⁡(ln⁡(2/δ)𝒲​Ns2​log2⁡(1/ϵ)){\cal O}\left(\frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{\sqrt{\cal W}}N_{s}^{2}\log_{2}(1/\epsilon)\right).

IV Probability weight of the RVB state within the BCS state

The probability weight of the RVB state within the BCS state is given by the square of the overlap between the two states.

𝒲=|⟨ψRVB|ψBCS⟩|2,\displaystyle{\cal W}=|\langle\psi_{\rm RVB}|\psi_{\rm BCS}\rangle|^{2}, (113)

where ψRVB\psi_{\rm RVB} and ψBCS\psi_{\rm BCS} denote the RVB and BCS wave functions, respectively. The wave function of the RVB state is related to that of the BCS state via the Gutzwiller projection:

|ψRVB⟩=𝒞𝒫G​|ψBCS⟩,\displaystyle|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle={\cal C}{\cal P}_{\rm G}|\psi_{\rm BCS}\rangle, (114)

where 𝒞{\cal C} is the normalization constant. We can calculate 𝒲{\cal W} based on its relationship with 𝒞{\cal C}:

𝒲=1/|𝒞|2.\displaystyle{\cal W}=1/|{\cal C}|^{2}. (115)

To understand why this is true, let us rewrite 𝒲{\cal W} in Eq. (113) as follows:

𝒲\displaystyle{\cal W} =|𝒞|2​|⟨ψBCS|𝒫G|ψBCS⟩|2\displaystyle=|{\cal C}|^{2}|\langle\psi_{\rm BCS}|{\cal P}_{\rm G}|\psi_{\rm BCS}\rangle|^{2}
=|𝒞|2​|⟨ψBCS|𝒫G2|ψBCS⟩|2,\displaystyle=|{\cal C}|^{2}|\langle\psi_{\rm BCS}|{\cal P}_{\rm G}^{2}|\psi_{\rm BCS}\rangle|^{2}, (116)

where we have used the fact that 𝒫G2=𝒫G{\cal P}_{G}^{2}={\cal P}_{G}. Then, by converting the BCS wave function back to the RVB wave function, one can rewrite Eq. (116) as follows:

𝒲\displaystyle{\cal W} =1|𝒞|2​|⟨ψRVB|ψRVB⟩|2,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|{\cal C}|^{2}}|\langle\psi_{\rm RVB}|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle|^{2}, (117)

which reduces to Eq. (115) due to the normalization of the RVB wave function.

The next step is to determine how to calculate 𝒞{\cal C}. To this end, let us examine exactly how 𝒫G{\cal P}_{G} operate on the BCS wave function, which can be expanded as follows:

|ψBCS⟩\displaystyle|\psi_{\rm BCS}\rangle =∑n∈GPHSan​|ϕn⟩+∑n∉GPHSan​|ϕn⟩,\displaystyle=\sum_{n\in\textrm{GPHS}}a_{n}|\phi_{n}\rangle+\sum_{n\notin\textrm{GPHS}}a_{n}|\phi_{n}\rangle, (118)

where {|ϕn⟩}\{|\phi_{n}\rangle\} is, at the moment, any convenient set of basis states, categorized into two groups: one group that is included in the Gutzwiller-projected Hilbert space (GPHS) and the other that is not. In other words, the first and second groups on the right side of Eq. (118) represent the components of the BCS wave function that survive and vanish after the application of 𝒫G{\cal P}_{\rm G}, respectively. In this representation, the RVB wave function can be represented by

|ψRVB⟩\displaystyle|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle =𝒞​∑n∈GPHSan​|ϕn⟩,\displaystyle={\cal C}\sum_{n\in\textrm{GPHS}}a_{n}|\phi_{n}\rangle, (119)

where 𝒞{\cal C} is the normalization constant that we aim to calculate.

It is now convenient to represent the BCS wave function using a set of basis states that distinguish the vacuum state from others. In this set of basis states, the amplitude of the vacuum state in the RVB wave function is given by 𝒞​a0{\cal C}a_{0}, where a0a_{0} refers to the amplitude of the vacuum state in the BCS wave function. As shown below, 𝒞{\cal C} can be calculated by taking the ratio of the amplitudes of the vacuum state in the RVB and BCS wave functions.

Suppose that we have the explicit form of the RVB wave function as follows:

|ψRVB⟩\displaystyle|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle =∑n∈GPHSbn​|ϕn⟩,\displaystyle=\sum_{n\in\textrm{GPHS}}b_{n}|\phi_{n}\rangle, (120)

where {bn}\{b_{n}\} are the amplitudes of the RVB wave function in the same set of basis states used to represent the BCS wave function, {|ϕn⟩}\{|\phi_{n}\rangle\}.

There is a particularly convenient set of basis states that can be formed by considering all possible arrangements of spin-up and spin-down electrons in a given lattice, subject to the no-double-occupancy constraint imposed by the Gutzwiller projection. Specifically, let us define |ϕn⟩|\phi_{n}\rangle as the nn-th configuration of electrons, where spin-up and spin-down electrons are distributed in the lattice sites at {𝐫↑,i(n)}\{{\bf r}^{(n)}_{\uparrow,i}\} and {𝐫↓,j(n)}\{{\bf r}^{(n)}_{\downarrow,j}\}, respectively, with ii and jj enumerating the lattice sites occupied by the corresponding spin species. Note that {𝐫↑,i(n)}\{{\bf r}^{(n)}_{\uparrow,i}\} and {𝐫↓,j(n)}\{{\bf r}^{(n)}_{\downarrow,j}\} are mutually exclusive due to the no-double-occupancy constraint. It is important to note that the total number of electrons can range from zero to the total number of lattice sites, covering all possible configurations from vacuum to half-filling.

It has been previously shown [25, 16] that, in this basis, the amplitudes of the RVB wave function can be expressed as follows, up to an overall normalization constant:

bn∝det⁡[φi​j(n)],\displaystyle b_{n}\propto{\rm det}[\varphi^{(n)}_{ij}], (121)

where φi​j(n)=φ⁡(𝐫↑,i(n)−𝐫↓,j(n))\varphi^{(n)}_{ij}=\varphi({\bf r}^{(n)}_{\uparrow,i}-{\bf r}^{(n)}_{\downarrow,j}) is the real-space component of the Cooper pair wave function with the constituent spin-up and spin-down electrons located at 𝐫↑,i(n){\bf r}^{(n)}_{\uparrow,i} and 𝐫↓,j(n){\bf r}^{(n)}_{\downarrow,j} in the nn-th configuration, respectively. Note that φ⁡(𝐫)\varphi({\bf r}) can be computed by performing the Fourier transform of v𝐤/u𝐤v_{\bf k}/u_{\bf k}, where u𝐤u_{\bf k} and v𝐤v_{\bf k} are the usual parameters of the BCS wave function,

u𝐤2=12​(1+ξ𝐤ξ𝐤2+Δ𝐤2)\displaystyle u^{2}_{\bf k}=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\frac{\xi_{\bf k}}{\sqrt{\xi^{2}_{\bf k}+\Delta^{2}_{\bf k}}}\right) (122)

and

v𝐤2=12​(1−ξ𝐤ξ𝐤2+Δ𝐤2)\displaystyle v^{2}_{\bf k}=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{\xi_{\bf k}}{\sqrt{\xi^{2}_{\bf k}+\Delta^{2}_{\bf k}}}\right) (123)

with ξ𝐤=ϵ𝐤−μ\xi_{\bf k}=\epsilon_{\bf k}-\mu being the difference between the kinetic energy and the chemical potential energy, and Δ𝐤\Delta_{\bf k} being the pairing amplitude. Here, we use the simple nearest-neighbor hopping model with ϵ𝐤=−2​t​(cos⁡kx+cos⁡ky)\epsilon_{\bf k}=-2t(\cos{k_{x}}+\cos{k_{y}}), where tt is the hopping parameter. Also, we focus on dd-wave superconductivity by setting Δ𝐤=2​Δ​(cos⁡kx−cos⁡ky)\Delta_{\bf k}=2\Delta(\cos{k_{x}}-\cos{k_{y}}), where Δ\Delta is the variational gap parameter.

Accounting for the overall normalization constant, the amplitudes of the nn-the configuration in the RVB wave function can be expressed as follows:

bn=𝒩​det​[φi​j(n)],\displaystyle b_{n}={\cal N}{\rm det}[\varphi^{(n)}_{ij}], (124)

where the normalization constant 𝒩{\cal N} is given by

1/𝒩=∑n∈GPHS|det⁡[φi​j(n)]|2.\displaystyle 1/{\cal N}=\sqrt{\sum_{n\in{\rm GPHS}}\left|{\rm det}[\varphi^{(n)}_{ij}]\right|^{2}}. (125)

This shows that the amplitude of the vacuum state in the RVB wave function is given by b0b_{0}, which is equivalent to 𝒩{\cal N} because the determinant part of the vacuum state is unity. In other words, we have b0=𝒩b_{0}={\cal N}.

By comparing Eqs. (119) and (120), it becomes evident that the amplitude of the vacuum state in the RVB wave function can be expressed in two distinct forms, which should ultimately be identical, so that

𝒞​a0=b0,\displaystyle{\cal C}a_{0}=b_{0}, (126)

or equivalently

𝒲=1/|𝒞|2=|a0/b0|2=|a0/𝒩|2,\displaystyle{\cal W}=1/|{\cal C}|^{2}=|a_{0}/b_{0}|^{2}=|a_{0}/{\cal N}|^{2}, (127)

indicating that 𝒲{\cal W} can be calculated once a0a_{0} and 𝒩{\cal N} are known.

Now, it is straightforward to determine a0a_{0} from the standard form of the BCS wave function:

|ψBCS⟩=∏𝐤(u𝐤+v𝐤​c𝐤,↑†​c−𝐤,↓†)​|0⟩,\displaystyle|\psi_{\rm BCS}\rangle=\prod_{\bf k}(u_{\bf k}+v_{\bf k}c^{\dagger}_{{\bf k},\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{-{\bf k},\downarrow})|0\rangle, (128)

where |0⟩|0\rangle is the vacuum state. The amplitude of the vacuum state is then given by

a0=∏𝐤u𝐤.\displaystyle a_{0}=\prod_{\bf k}u_{\bf k}. (129)

Combining everything together, the probability weight of the RVB state within the BCS state is finally given by

𝒲=∏𝐤u𝐤2​(∑n∈GPHS|det⁡[φi​j(n)]|2),\displaystyle{\cal W}=\prod_{\bf k}u^{2}_{\bf k}\left(\sum_{n\in{\rm GPHS}}\left|{\rm det}[\varphi^{(n)}_{ij}]\right|^{2}\right), (130)

which is uniquely determined by the variational gap parameter Δ\Delta and the chemical potential μ\mu.

We aim to calculate 𝒲{\cal W} when the RVB state is relevant to high-temperature superconductivity. We consider the uniform tt-JJ model on a square lattice which can be derived from the infinite repulsion limit of an on-site Hubbard model [5]. The tt-JJ model is expected to harbor critical features observed in high-temperature superconductors and may also contain the fundamental mechanism underlying pairing from repulsion. The tt-JJ model is also more efficient than the Hubbard model to implement in quantum algorithms [32].

To find 𝒲{\cal W} we must accurately construct the BCS input parameters. Specifically, we must find Δ\Delta as a function of hole doping concentration, xx, that maximizes the overlap between the RVB state and the exact ground state of the tt-JJ model at each xx. Note that we initially calculate the overlap between the RVB state and the exact ground state of the tt-JJ model at specified values of Δ\Delta and μ\mu, and then convert it to a function of Δ\Delta and xx.

The overlap between the RVB state and the exact ground state of the tt-JJ model can be computed using straightforward exact diagonalization methods, such as the modified Lanczos method. However, there is a subtlety in properly defining the overlap due to the inherent fluctuations in particle number in the RVB state. Specifically, the RVB state can be expressed as a sum of its particle-number components as follows:

|ψRVB⟩=∑NλN​|ϕRVBN⟩,|\psi_{\rm RVB}\rangle=\sum_{N}\lambda_{N}|\phi^{N}_{\rm RVB}\rangle, (131)

where λN\lambda_{N} and |ϕRVBN⟩|\phi^{N}_{\rm RVB}\rangle denote the amplitude and the component of the RVB state in the specific particle-number sector with NN particles, respectively. On the other hand, the exact ground state of the tt-JJ model exhibits no such fluctuations. To account for this difference, we define proper overlap as the average of the square of the overlap between the two states in each particle-number sector NN, weighted by the probability weight |λN|2|\lambda_{N}|^{2} [25]:

𝒪2¯=∑N|λN|2​|⟨ϕRVBN|ϕt​-​JN⟩|2,\overline{{\cal O}^{2}}=\sum_{N}|\lambda_{N}|^{2}|\langle\phi^{N}_{\rm RVB}|\phi^{N}_{t\mbox{-}J}\rangle|^{2}, (132)

where |ϕt​-​JN⟩|\phi^{N}_{t\mbox{-}J}\rangle is the exact ground state of the tt-JJ model in the sector with NN particles. For simplicity, we will refer to 𝒪2¯\overline{{\cal O}^{2}} as simply the overlap from now on.

Figure 4 presents the results of numerical analyses to determine 𝒲{\cal W} across various finite-size systems up to the maximum obtainable within classical memory constraints. Specifically, panels (a), (b), and (c) in Fig. 4 show the phase diagram of the overlap as a function of Δ\Delta and xx for finite-size systems with the number of states, Ns=10N_{s}=10, 1818, and 2020, respectively. We calculate 𝒲{\cal W} along the green curves, where the overlap is maximized at each xx. Panels (d), (e), and (f) in Fig. 4 show log⁡𝒲\log{\cal W} as a function of xx along the maximum-overlap curves for Ns=10N_{s}=10, 1818, and 2020, respectively. Finally, panel (g) shows that log⁡𝒲\log{\cal W} scales linearly with NsN_{s} for various values of xx. Consequently, 𝒲{\cal W} can be expressed as follows:

𝒲=𝒜​e−λ​Ns,{\cal W}={\cal A}e^{-\lambda N_{s}}, (133)

where 𝒜{\cal A} and λ\lambda denote the exponential prefactor and the decay constant of 𝒲{\cal W}, which depends on the hole doping concentration xx. For x=0.1x=0.1, 0.20.2, 0.30.3, and 0.40.4, 𝒜{\cal A} is 3.04523.0452, 0.83590.8359, 0.63730.6373, and 0.52280.5228, and λ\lambda is 0.58610.5861, 0.33820.3382, 0.20750.2075, and 0.10920.1092, respectively.

This means that, for example, at Ns=100N_{s}=100, 𝒲≃1.7×10−15{\cal W}\simeq 1.7\times 10^{-15} for x=0.2x=0.2, which yields the largest pairing gap and is therefore considered as optimal doping within the RVB framework. Note that Ns=100N_{s}=100 is sufficiently large to exhibit near-thermodynamic behavior. Using the measurement-based projection algorithm, this would require checking for double occupancy at every site an order of 101510^{15} times to achieve the Gutzwiller projection. On the other hand, using the AAGP algorithm developed in this work, the Gutzwiller projection can be achieved by applying 𝒰BCS{\cal U}_{\rm BCS} and 𝒰BCS−1{\cal U}^{-1}_{\rm BCS} (with each accompanied by an appropriate conditional unitary operator) only an order of 10710^{7} or 10810^{8} times.

V SUMMARY AND OUTLOOK

In this work, we have constructed scalable quantum algorithms for implementing the Gutzwiller projection via amplitude amplification. The AAGP algorithm constructed here reduces the number of qubit operations by many orders of magnitude compared with the measurement-based projection algorithm, thereby making it a potentially useful input-state preparation primitive for quantum algorithms targeting strongly correlated models. The key point is not only the asymptotic quadratic reduction from 𝒪⁡(1/𝒲){\cal O}(1/{\cal W}) to 𝒪⁡(1/𝒲){\cal O}(1/\sqrt{\cal W}), but also that, in the regime benchmarked here, this reduction is large enough to cross a practical finite-size threshold. For projected BCS/RVB states relevant to our test case, the improvement changes the state-preparation step from effectively unusable to plausibly deployable at lattice sizes of physical interest.

We emphasize, however, that AAGP by itself does not resolve the full resource challenge of simulating strongly correlated models. Rather, it removes a key obstruction in preparing a physically motivated class of input states. This distinction is important because the usefulness of many quantum simulation algorithms depends sensitively on the choice of the initial state, and projected BCS/RVB states provide a flexible ansatz family for strongly correlated Hubbard, tt-JJ, and related spin models. In this sense, AAGP should be viewed as an enabling primitive within a broader fault-tolerant workflow.

The finite-size regime emphasized here is already nontrivial. The scaling analysis suggests that the input RVB state remains meaningful when extrapolated to lattice sizes on the order of 100 sites, where direct classical overlap calculations are no longer feasible. Thus, although the exponentially small RVB weight continues to govern the asymptotic cost, the quadratic improvement is sufficient to make an important difference at the physically relevant finite sizes that motivate quantum simulation in the first place.

The initial states discussed here strictly enforce Gutzwiller projection, but this can be relaxed. No double occupancy is precisely the limit assumed by the tt-JJ model, where the system is simplified by taking the on-site repulsive interaction, UU, to be infinitely large. A natural question is whether it is possible to build a similar ansatz for the ground states of Hubbard models that allow the controlled addition of double occupancies. One possible extension is to use AAGP and then perform a systematic unitary transformation on the Gutzwiller-projected BCS state to perturbatively account for the effects of double occupancy within the t/Ut/U expansion of the Hubbard model. Specifically, we can modify the Gutzwiller-projected BCS state to incorporate the effects of double occupancy perturbatively [35]:

|ψ⟩=ei​S​𝒫G​|ψBCS⟩,|\psi\rangle=e^{iS}{\cal P}_{\rm G}|\psi_{\rm BCS}\rangle, (134)

where the unitary transformation ei​Se^{iS} can be derived systematically via the t/Ut/U expansion of the Hubbard model [15, 28]. Developing efficient quantum algorithms for this unitary transformation would be valuable in future research.

Appendix A Redundancy in the Bloch-Messiah decomposition

The Bloch-Messiah decomposition contains redundancy, so that different forms of 𝐃|n+2​p\mathbf{D}|_{n+2p} can yield the same BCS state. Specifically, the BCS state in Eq. (13) is invariant under the following SU⁡(n)\mathrm{SU}(n) transformation acting on unpaired states:

f~i†={∑j=1n[𝐌]j​i​fj†if ​1≤i≤n,fi†if ​i>n,\displaystyle\tilde{f}_{i}^{\dagger}=\begin{cases}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n}[\mathbf{M}]_{ji}f_{j}^{\dagger}\qquad\textrm{if }1\leq i\leq n,\\ f_{i}^{\dagger}\qquad\qquad\qquad\textrm{if }i>n,\end{cases} (135)

where 𝐌∈SU⁡(n)\mathbf{M}\in\mathrm{SU}(n). This invariance is due to the fact that f~1†​…​f~n†=f1†​…​fn†\tilde{f}_{1}^{\dagger}\ldots\tilde{f}_{n}^{\dagger}=f_{1}^{\dagger}\ldots f_{n}^{\dagger}. In matrix form, the above SU⁡(n)\mathrm{SU}(n) transformation acts on 𝐃|n+2​p\mathbf{D}|_{n+2p} as follows:

𝐃|n+2​p↦𝐃|n+2​p​(𝐌𝟏2​p×2​p),\mathbf{D}|_{n+2p}\mapsto\mathbf{D}|_{n+2p}\left(\begin{array}[]{c|c}\mathbf{M}&\\ \cline{1-2}\cr&\mathbf{1}_{2p\times 2p}\end{array}\right), (136)

which can be in turn used to make [𝐃|n+2​p]i​j=0[\mathbf{D}|_{n+2p}]_{ij}=0 for i−j>N−ni-j>N-n.

For example, when N=6N=6, n=3n=3, and p=1p=1, 𝐌\mathbf{M} can be chosen such that

As mentioned in the main text, the procedure above can be generalized to show [𝐃|n+2​p]i​j=0[\mathbf{D}|_{n+2p}]_{ij}=0 for i−j>N−ni-j>N-n.

Appendix B Two-qubit gate number and circuit depth of the BCS quantum circuit

In this appendix, we calculate the two-qubit gate number and the circuit depth of the BCS quantum circuit. To begin, it is important to note that our BCS quantum circuit constructs the full BCS state using two distinct groups of two-qubit gate operations. The first group is associated with Givens rotations, as described in Eqs. (II.1) and (II.1), while the second group is associated with the creation of Cooper pairs in the depth-1 BCS state, as described in Eq. (74). The first group can be further divided into two additional subgroups: Givens rotations involving (i) unpaired states and (ii) paired states.

Generalizing the example given in the main text using Eqs. (II.1) and (II.1), we can illustrate our BCS quantum circuit with a schematic diagram shown in Fig. 5. As one can see from Fig. 5, the two-qubit gate number for Givens rotations involving unpaired states is S1=n⁡(N−n)S_{1}=n(N-n), while that for Givens rotations involving paired states is

S2\displaystyle S_{2} =∑k=12​p(N−n−k)\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{2p}(N-n-k)
=2​p​(N−n)−p⁡(2​p+1).\displaystyle=2p(N-n)-p(2p+1). (194)

In the meantime, the two-qubit gate number associated with the creation of Cooper pairs in the depth-1 BCS state is simply S3=pS_{3}=p. When all the groups are combined, the total number of two-qubit gates is given as follows:

Stot\displaystyle S_{\rm tot} =S1+S2+S3\displaystyle=S_{1}+S_{2}+S_{3}
=(N−n)​(n+2​p)−2​p2.\displaystyle=(N-n)(n+2p)-2p^{2}. (195)

Finally, the circuit depth is given by the horizontal length of the quantum circuit in Fig. 5:

L=N+2​p.\displaystyle L=N+2p. (196)

Appendix C Solution of the amplitude amplification recursion relation

Here, we demonstrate that the recursion relation in Eq. (105) has the solution in Eq. (107). To this end, let us consider the following recursion relation:

an=x⁡(1−ei​ϕn−1)​an−1+ei​ϕn−1​an−2,a_{n}=x(1-e^{i\phi_{n-1}})a_{n-1}+e^{i\phi_{n-1}}a_{n-2}, (197)

where

ϕn≡2​cot−1⁡(1−γ2​tan⁡n​πL)\phi_{n}\equiv 2\cot^{-1}\left(\sqrt{1-\gamma^{2}}\tan{\frac{n\pi}{L}}\right) (198)

with γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) and LL being an integer. Then, given the initial condiction (a0,a1)=(1,x)(a_{0},a_{1})=(1,x), it has been previously shown [45] that

aL=TL​(x/γ)TL​(1/γ),a_{L}=\frac{T_{L}(x/\gamma)}{T_{L}(1/\gamma)}, (199)

where TLT_{L} is the LL-th Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind.

What we aim to demonstrate is that the recursion relation in Eq. (197) is equivalent to that in Eq. (105) when considering only an odd number of iteration steps. To this end, let us rewrite Eq. (105) as follows:

bn=1−x2​(ei​φn−1−1)​bn−1+ei​φn−1​bn−2,b_{n}=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}(e^{i\varphi_{n-1}}-1)b_{n-1}+e^{i\varphi_{n-1}}b_{n-2}, (200)

where φn=(−1)n−1​ϕn\varphi_{n}=(-1)^{n-1}\phi_{n} and x=1−𝒲x=\sqrt{1-{\cal W}}. The final goal is to prove that

bL=exp⁡(i​∑n=1(L−1)/2φ2​n)​TL​(x/γ)TL​(1/γ),b_{L}=\exp{\left(i\sum_{n=1}^{(L-1)/2}\varphi_{2n}\right)}\frac{T_{L}(x/\gamma)}{T_{L}(1/\gamma)}, (201)

given the initial condition (b0,b1)=(0,x)(b_{0},b_{1})=(0,x)

Proof: We utilize mathematical induction based on the index nn. The n=1n=1 case is trivial, and the n=3n=3 case can be proven by brute force. Suppose that our claim holds for all positive odd integers less than or equal to some odd integer n≥3n\geq 3. Then, we can apply Eq. (200) multiple times to obtain the recursion relation that involves only odd indices, i.e., bn+2b_{n+2}, bnb_{n}, and bn−2b_{n-2}:

bn+2\displaystyle b_{n+2} =1−x2​(ei​φn+1−1)​bn+1+ei​φn+1​bn\displaystyle=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}(e^{i\varphi_{n+1}}-1)b_{n+1}+e^{i\varphi_{n+1}}b_{n}
=1−x2​(e−i​ϕn+1−1)​[1−x2​(ei​ϕn−1)​bn+ei​ϕn​bn−1]+e−i​ϕn+1​bn\displaystyle=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}(e^{-i\phi_{n+1}}-1)\left[\sqrt{1-x^{2}}(e^{i\phi_{n}}-1)b_{n}+e^{i\phi_{n}}b_{n-1}\right]+e^{-i\phi_{n+1}}b_{n}
=e−i​ϕn+1​[1−(1−ei​ϕn+1)​(1−ei​ϕn)​(1−x2)]​bn−(1−e−i​ϕn+1)​ei​ϕn​1−x2​bn−1\displaystyle=e^{-i\phi_{n+1}}\left[1-(1-e^{i\phi_{n+1}})(1-e^{i\phi_{n}})(1-x^{2})\right]b_{n}-(1-e^{-i\phi_{n+1}})e^{i\phi_{n}}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}b_{n-1}
=e−i​ϕn+1​[1−(1−ei​ϕn+1)​(1−ei​ϕn)​(1−x2)]​bn−e−i​ϕn+1​(1−ei​ϕn+1)​ei​ϕn​bn−e−i​ϕn−1​bn−21−e−i​ϕn−1,\displaystyle=e^{-i\phi_{n+1}}\left[1-(1-e^{i\phi_{n+1}})(1-e^{i\phi_{n}})(1-x^{2})\right]b_{n}-e^{-i\phi_{n+1}}(1-e^{i\phi_{n+1}})e^{i\phi_{n}}\frac{b_{n}-e^{-i\phi_{n-1}}b_{n-2}}{1-e^{-i\phi_{n-1}}}, (202)

where we have used the induction hypothesis. Let us now define b~n=ei⁡(ϕ2+ϕ4+…​ϕn−1)​bn\tilde{b}_{n}=e^{i(\phi_{2}+\phi_{4}+\ldots\phi_{n-1})}b_{n}, which satisfies the following recursion relation:

b~n+2\displaystyle\tilde{b}_{n+2} =[1−(1−ei​ϕn+1)​(1−ei​ϕn)​(1−x2)]​b~n−(1−ei​ϕn+1)​ei​ϕn​b~n−b~n−21−e−i​ϕn−1\displaystyle=\left[1-(1-e^{i\phi_{n+1}})(1-e^{i\phi_{n}})(1-x^{2})\right]\tilde{b}_{n}-(1-e^{i\phi_{n+1}})e^{i\phi_{n}}\frac{\tilde{b}_{n}-\tilde{b}_{n-2}}{1-e^{-i\phi_{n-1}}}
=[(1−ei​ϕn+1)​(1−ei​ϕn)​x2+ei​ϕn+1]​b~n+(1−ei​ϕn+1)​ei​ϕn​b~n−ei​ϕn−1​b~n−21−ei​ϕn−1,\displaystyle=\left[(1-e^{i\phi_{n+1}})(1-e^{i\phi_{n}})x^{2}+e^{i\phi_{n+1}}\right]\tilde{b}_{n}+(1-e^{i\phi_{n+1}})e^{i\phi_{n}}\frac{\tilde{b}_{n}-e^{i\phi_{n-1}}\tilde{b}_{n-2}}{1-e^{i\phi_{n-1}}}, (203)

We can perform similar calculations to obtain the recursion relation involving an+2a_{n+2}, ana_{n}, and an−2a_{n-2} by using Eq. (197):

an+2\displaystyle a_{n+2} =x⁡(1−ei​ϕn+1)​an+1+ei​ϕn+1​an\displaystyle=x(1-e^{i\phi_{n+1}})a_{n+1}+e^{i\phi_{n+1}}a_{n}
=x⁡(1−ei​ϕn+1)​[x⁡(1−ei​ϕn)​an+ei​ϕn​an−1]+ei​ϕn+1​an\displaystyle=x(1-e^{i\phi_{n+1}})\left[x(1-e^{i\phi_{n}})a_{n}+e^{i\phi_{n}}a_{n-1}\right]+e^{i\phi_{n+1}}a_{n}
=[(1−ei​ϕn+1)​(1−ei​ϕn)​x2+ei​ϕn+1]​an+(1−ei​ϕn+1)​ei​ϕn​x​an−1\displaystyle=\left[(1-e^{i\phi_{n+1}})(1-e^{i\phi_{n}})x^{2}+e^{i\phi_{n+1}}\right]a_{n}+(1-e^{i\phi_{n+1}})e^{i\phi_{n}}xa_{n-1}
=[(1−ei​ϕn+1)​(1−ei​ϕn)​x2+ei​ϕn+1]​an+(1−ei​ϕn+1)​ei​ϕn​an−ei​ϕn−1​an−21−ei​ϕn−1.\displaystyle=\left[(1-e^{i\phi_{n+1}})(1-e^{i\phi_{n}})x^{2}+e^{i\phi_{n+1}}\right]a_{n}+(1-e^{i\phi_{n+1}})e^{i\phi_{n}}\frac{a_{n}-e^{i\phi_{n-1}}a_{n-2}}{1-e^{i\phi_{n-1}}}. (204)

As one can see from the comparison between Eqs. (203) and (204), ana_{n} and b~n\tilde{b}_{n} satisfy the same recursion relation for odd indices. Therefore, an=b~n=ei⁡(ϕ2+ϕ4+…​ϕn−1)​bna_{n}=\tilde{b}_{n}=e^{i(\phi_{2}+\phi_{4}+\ldots\phi_{n-1})}b_{n}. Noting that ϕn=−φn\phi_{n}=-\varphi_{n} for even nn, we can finally prove Eq. (201).

Appendix D Optimization of the iteration length for amplitude amplification

We begin with the following condition described in the main text:

1−𝒲/γ≤1.\displaystyle\sqrt{1-{\cal W}}/\gamma\leq 1. (205)

Above, γ\gamma is related to the desired tolerance, δ\delta, as follows:

TL​(1/γ)=1/δ,\displaystyle T_{L}(1/\gamma)=1/\delta, (206)

where TLT_{L} is the LL-th Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind.

Equation (205) can be rewritten as follows:

𝒲≥1−[T1/L​(1/δ)]−2,\displaystyle{\cal W}\geq 1-[T_{1/L}(1/\delta)]^{-2}, (207)

where we have utilized the inverse of Eq. (206):

1/γ=T1/L​(1/δ).\displaystyle 1/\gamma=T_{1/L}(1/\delta). (208)

Note that Eq. (208) can be obtained from the definition of the Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind:

Tn​(x)={cos⁡(n​cos−1⁡(x))if ​|x|≤1cosh⁡(n​cosh−1⁡(x))if ​|x|>1\displaystyle T_{n}(x)=\begin{cases}\cos{(n\cos^{-1}{(x)})}&\text{if }|x|\leq 1\\ \cosh{(n\cosh^{-1}{(x)})}&\text{if }|x|>1\end{cases} (209)

Now, assuming that L≫1L\gg 1 and δ≪1\delta\ll 1, we can expand T1/L​(1/δ)T_{1/L}(1/\delta) as shown below:

T1/L​(1/δ)\displaystyle T_{1/L}(1/\delta) =cosh⁡(1L​cosh−1⁡(1/δ))\displaystyle=\cosh{\left(\frac{1}{L}\cosh^{-1}(1/\delta)\right)}
≈1+12​(1L​cosh−1⁡(1/δ))2.\displaystyle\approx 1+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{L}\cosh^{-1}(1/\delta)\right)^{2}. (210)

Next, we can also expand cosh−1⁡(1/δ)\cosh^{-1}(1/\delta) as follows:

cosh−1⁡(1/δ)≈ln⁡(2/δ),\displaystyle\cosh^{-1}(1/\delta)\approx\ln(2/\delta), (211)

which can be proved by applying the hyperbolic cosine function to both sides of the equation. Then, Equation (210) can be rewritten as follows:

T1/L​(1/δ)≈1+12​(ln⁡(2/δ)L)2,\displaystyle T_{1/L}(1/\delta)\approx 1+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\ln{(2/\delta)}}{L}\right)^{2}, (212)

which can, in turn, be plugged into Eq. (207) to generate the following condition:

𝒲≥(ln⁡(2/δ)L)2.\displaystyle{\cal W}\geq\left(\frac{\ln{(2/\delta)}}{L}\right)^{2}. (213)

Finally, Equation (213) reduces to the following expression of the optimization condition for LL:

L≥ln⁡(2/δ)𝒲.L\geq\frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{\sqrt{{\cal W}}}. (214)
